description: We are a multidisciplinary team of five passionate innovators skilled in AI/ML, software development, electronics, embedded systems, data analysis, and research. We aim to build an innovative astronaut health monitoring solution using NASA data and emerging technologies. We welcome participants with skills in biomedical/health sciences, UI/UX, backend/cloud development, or space science to strengthen our team.
summary: ASTRA (AI-Driven Crew Cognitive State Monitoring and Early Warning System) is an AI-powered prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The project uses NASA's publicly available Flight Crew Physiological Data for Crew State Monitoring dataset to analyse physiological signals, including EEG, ECG, respiration, and Galvanic Skin Response (GSR). It uses a trained Random Forest machine learning model to classify physiological data patterns into two categories: Baseline Cognitive State and Elevated Cognitive Load. The system presents these predictions through an interactive dashboard that visualizes physiological information and provides visual alerts when elevated cognitive load is detected. ASTRA addresses the challenge of monitoring crew cognitive workload in demanding aviation and spaceflight environments. It is important because identifying patterns associated with elevated cognitive load could support research into crew performance, situational awareness, and operational safety. The project is a research prototype and is not intended for medical diagnosis or certified operational safety decisions.
details:
Project Description: ASTRA

ASTRA (AI-Driven Crew Cognitive State Monitoring and Early Warning System) is a machine learning-based prototype designed to monitor physiological patterns associated with elevated cognitive workload in demanding aviation and spaceflight environments.

How It Works

ASTRA processes physiological data from NASA's publicly available Flight Crew Physiological Data for Crew State Monitoring dataset. The data includes Electroencephalography (EEG), Electrocardiography (ECG), respiration, and Galvanic Skin Response (GSR). The system processes 30-second data windows, extracts 36 physiological features, and uses a trained Random Forest classifier to estimate whether the observed patterns represent a Baseline Cognitive State or Elevated Cognitive Load. The model generates a probability score, which is used to determine the predicted state. An interactive dashboard presents physiological trends, prediction results, historical data, and visual early-warning alerts.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRA explores how artificial intelligence and physiological signal analysis can support the understanding of crew cognitive workload. Identifying patterns associated with elevated cognitive load could help researchers investigate attention, situational awareness, and decision-making under demanding operational conditions. Its intended impact is to contribute to future research into crew monitoring technologies for aviation and space exploration.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Programming language: Python, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS.
  • Machine Learning: Scikit-learn and Random Forest Classifier.
  • Data processing: Pandas, NumPy, and SciPy.
  • Model management: Joblib.
  • Backend: FastAPI and Uvicorn.
  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, Vanilla JavaScript, and SVG-based visualizations.
  • Data source: NASA Flight Crew Physiological Data for Crew State Monitoring.
  • Development environment: Python-based development tools and GitHub for source-code management.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of ASTRA is its integration of multiple physiological signal types into a single cognitive-state monitoring platform. Instead of relying on one physiological measurement, it combines brain activity, cardiac information, respiration, and skin conductance to identify patterns associated with elevated cognitive load. Another important aspect is the integration of an existing trained machine learning model with an interactive dashboard that makes model predictions easier to interpret.

Factors Considered

During development, we considered the availability of publicly accessible and labelled physiological datasets, signal quality, feature extraction, differences between individuals, model performance, and the limitations of applying pilot data to astronaut-related research. Our initial concept focused on orthostatic intolerance monitoring, but the lack of a suitable publicly accessible labelled astronaut cardiovascular dataset led us to focus on cognitive-state monitoring using the NASA data available to us.

The current model achieved a ROC-AUC of 0.626 during Leave-One-Subject-Out evaluation. We acknowledge that further validation with larger and more diverse datasets is necessary. The current system uses recorded physiological data and is not yet integrated with live sensors. It is a research prototype, not a medical diagnostic or certified operational safety system.
